hook.text: In 1988, a grad student released a program that accidentally crippled 10% of the entire internet.

buildup.text: Robert Morris built a worm to measure the internet's size. It exploited Unix flaws to spread between machines.

discovery.text: A bug made it reinfect the same machines repeatedly. Each copy ate resources until systems crashed.

twist.text: About 6,000 machines — 10% of the internet — were hit. Damage was estimated at $10 million.

climax.text: The incident created CERT, the first computer emergency response team, at Carnegie Mellon University.

punchline.text: One student's experiment launched the field of internet security.

quiz.question: What unintended behavior made the Morris Worm so destructive?
options: It reinfected the same machines repeatedly, crashing them
It deleted all files on infected computers
It sent spam email to every contact

details.summary: The Morris Worm was the first major internet worm, released by Robert Tappan Morris in 1988. It exploited Unix vulnerabilities and infected roughly 6,000 machines, about 10 percent of the internet. The incident led to the creation of CERT, the first computer emergency response team.
details.whyItMatters: The Morris Worm proved that a single piece of code could cripple a global network. It birthed the field of internet security and the coordinated incident response model still used today.
takeaways: The Morris Worm infected 10% of the 1988 internet
It led to the creation of CERT for coordinated response
Morris became the first person convicted under the CFAA

faq.question: How did the Morris Worm spread so quickly?
faq.answer: It exploited multiple Unix vulnerabilities including sendmail, fingerd, and rsh. A bug in its replication logic caused it to re-infect machines already compromised, consuming resources exponentially. The internet had no defenses against self-replicating code at that time.

faq.question: What lasting impact did the Morris Worm have?
faq.answer: It created the field of internet security as a discipline. CERT was established at Carnegie Mellon to coordinate responses. The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act was strengthened. Network administrators began taking security seriously for the first time.
